hints: Remember how addition polymers form, the C=C double bond of the alkene opens up to make two new single bonds in the chain, so try reversing that idea.
Put the double bond back between the two backbone carbons to get $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$, which is a straight chain of five carbons.
Now name that 5-carbon alkene by giving the double bond the lowest possible number to finish the job.
walkthrough:
**Reverse the polymerisation**

Think of the repeat unit as an opened-out alkene. To find the monomer, join the two backbone carbons with a double bond and remove the continuation bonds.

$$-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CH}(\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3)- \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$$

**Draw out the full monomer**

Great, you now have the monomer skeleton. Count the longest carbon chain containing the double bond.

There are 5 carbons in a row: C1 is the $\text{CH}_3$ on the left, C2 and C3 are the $\text{CH}=$ carbons, then C4 is $\text{CH}_2$ and C5 is $\text{CH}_3$ on the right.

**Give the correct IUPAC name**

A 5-carbon alkene is a pentene. Number from the end that gives the double bond the lowest locant.

The double bond starts at carbon 2, so the name is pent-2-ene.

options.A: Not correct. 1-methyl-2-ethylethene tries to name ethene with two substituents, but this breaks the IUPAC rule to choose the longest continuous chain containing the double bond. The longest chain here is 5 carbons, not 2.
options.B: Not correct. 1-ethylprop-1-ene also fails the longest chain rule. The three-carbon propene parent is too short because you can include the ethyl group to make a continuous five-carbon chain, which must be chosen instead.
options.C: Correct. The monomer is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$. This is a straight chain of five carbons with the double bond starting at carbon 2, so the systematic name is pent-2-ene.
options.D: Not correct. Pent-1-ene would be $\text{CH}_2=\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, which would polymerise to $-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}(\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3)-$. That has only one branched side chain, not the two side groups ($\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$) seen in the question.
